extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history; historians; scholars of print culture
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and guidance about producing and reading early-18th-century printed advertisements (rhetoric, layout, claims, and social uses) with historical examples from newspapers and periodicals of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boastful claims and wagers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of extravagant boasts and formal wagers (e.g., 'lay 20 guineas to their 10') in advertisements to assert superiority or settle disputes about workmanship or product quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Willdey & Brandreth offering bets against rivals; the text shows such public challenges used to persuade readers of confidence and quality. Anti-pattern: such bragging can be seen as mountebankery if unsupported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical demonstration / comparative trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide opportunities for direct comparison or public trial of products (e.g., inviting 'any gentleman that will may see the experiment tried ... at our shop').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance in the text: offering to compare instruments on the spot or staging tests is a way to remove pretension and convince skeptical customers. Example: sellers buying rivals' instruments to prove superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority endorsements and certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite approval or certificates from respected bodies or experts (e.g., 'shewed to the Royal Society ... and by them approved').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marshall's certificate from the Royal Society is used to legitimise his claim. Using authoritative endorsement bolsters credibility; absence or falsity of such claims is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of testimony and oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on witness testimony, oaths, or sworn statements from customers or bystanders to support claims (e.g., 'several persons ... have offered to give their oaths').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records advertisers offering oaths and witness evidence to counter rival slanders. Such social proof functions as verification in the absence of formal regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness versus mountebankery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid falsehoods, overblown mountebank-style promises, and deceptive boasting; truthful, demonstrable claims are defended and praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts 'mountebanks' and genuine improvement; passages call out 'lying vaunt' and 'falsehood'. Anti-patterns: extravagant unverifiable claims ('micro-scope the same that any one may have from Culpeper') are subject to public rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye-catching typographic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typographic ornament and devices to catch the reader's eye: asterisks, pointing hands, 'N.B.', little cuts and figures, and the 'blind Italian character' (deliberately hard-to-read type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison notes these methods as 'the great art in writing advertisements'—they 'fix and detain the eye.' The passage attributes some inventions (cuts/figures) to particular advertisers (spring-truss author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornate / elevated rhetorical style
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a florid or classical ('Ciceronian') style and grandiloquent phrases ('universal esteem', 'most glorious') to impress readers and convey worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator and other periodicals printed highly ornate product descriptions as persuasive devices. Example: 'The highest compounded Spirit of Lavender ... which so raptures the spirits.' Warning: style can mask substance and invite satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency and cleanliness of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain decorous wording in advertisements — avoid gross, indecent, or overly graphic terms that would offend polite readers (e.g., criticism of 'Carminative Wind-Expelling Pills').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison admonishes advertisers to avoid coarse phrasing; failing to do so damages the perceived decency of the paper and may provoke censure. Anti-pattern: using crude descriptive terms even if accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and digesting of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful ordering and grouping of advertisements (the bookseller's arrangement) makes the collection coherent and usable (e.g., grouping by product or notice type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison reproduces a sample ordering ('Spanish blacking', 'beautifying cream', 'Pease and Plasters', etc.) and attributes part of the bookseller's craft to how ads are ranged and digested for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements as instruments of social ambition/status
rubrics_metrics.description: Use advertisements to assert social standing or ambition by appearing alongside news and dignified notices—positioning tradespeople 'in the same paper of news with a plenipotentiary'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison observes that adverts serve as instruments of ambition, allowing lesser persons to 'creep into the Gazette' and gain prominence. This rhetorical placement is itself a persuasive strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advertisements for controversy and polemics
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ advertisements as platforms for quarrels, denunciations, and rivalries (e.g., long bitter exchanges among strop-makers, pill proprietors, instrument-makers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes 'above half the advertisements ... are purely polemical' in some cases; while effective at drawing attention, this use can be 'aggressional and objectionable trade purposes' and damage reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear practical information (where to procure goods/services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include precise, usable information about where and how goods or services can be obtained (addresses, shop signs, prices, terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison lists this as a principal utility of adverts: 'to inform the world where they may be furnished with almost every thing.' Examples include specific shop addresses, prices, and directions for contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid placement and the business of ad-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that advertisements are paid insertions and that professional ad-writing/agency services may be offered for a fee ('sent to me with five shillings to be inserted').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents in the Spectator propose monopolising ad-writing and note that advertisers purchase placement; this shapes style and content (and can produce formulaic 'patterns of good writing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intermediaries and classified/private notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ intermediaries, initials, or instructions for private replies (e.g., 'letter directed to Mr Samuel Reeves ... to be left with Mr May') to enable discrete communication or classified notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gentleman asking when he may wait on a lady uses a forwarding address; this preserves privacy and was a common form for personal notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming novelty or invention — be prepared to prove it
rubrics_metrics.description: Assert invention or novel improvements only with evidence; rivals will publicly challenge and demand proof (e.g., claims about microscopes and 'two-foot telescopes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter recounts disputes where claimants offered wagers, bought rivals' instruments for test, and relied on certificates or witnesses. Anti-pattern: unsupported claims invite reputational harm and public rebuttal.
